node-1.label: A 54-year-old man presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain and shortness of breath

node-2.label: Patient has a medical history of hypertension and subglottic squamous cell carcinoma, treated with cisplatin and radiation therapy 8 months prior

node-3.label: Physical examination showed signs of respiratory distress; the patient rapidly deteriorated, requiring intubation and hemodynamic support with norepinephrine, phenylephrine, and vasopressin

node-4.label: Hospital course lasted 2 months and was complicated by pulmonary embolism, atrial fibrillation, and gastrointestinal bleeding

why.why: Both radiology and laboratory expert analyses explicitly favor an acute cardiopulmonary event as the leading explanation. Negative blood and fluid cultures exclude abdominal sepsis, while confirmed pulmonary embolism, new atrial fibrillation, and shock/respiratory failure provide strong clinical support. Echocardiography, CTPA, cardiac biomarkers, and ECG remain pending, so confidence is increased modestly from 0.65 to 0.70.

The laboratory expert analysis explicitly states that negative blood and fluid cultures refute abdominal sepsis. With no alternative culture or imaging evidence of intra-abdominal infection, the sepsis hypothesis is essentially excluded; confidence is reduced from 0.05 to 0.02.

The laboratory expert analysis states that the current evidence and clinical course align with an acute cardiopulmonary mechanism over treatment-related toxicity. The remote cisplatin/radiation history does not explain the acute thromboembolic and cardiac events as well as PE with right heart strain; confidence is reduced from 0.12 to 0.10.

Neither expert analysis supports tumor recurrence/metastasis as the cause of the acute deterioration, and the laboratory analysis explicitly favors a cardiopulmonary mechanism over tumor progression. The acute PE, atrial fibrillation, and shock are better explained by an acute cardiopulmonary event; confidence is reduced from 0.08 to 0.05.

node-9.label: Echocardiography, CT pulmonary angiography, cardiac biomarkers, and ECG have been requested but results are not yet available

node-10.label: The acute cardiopulmonary event may be due to pulmonary embolism with right heart strain and/or myocardial injury

why.why: Radiology and laboratory analyses both identify PE with right heart strain as the leading mechanism, supported by confirmed PE, shock, respiratory failure, and negative cultures that exclude sepsis. Because echocardiography, CTPA, cardiac biomarkers, and ECG are still pending, right heart strain and myocardial injury cannot yet be definitively confirmed; confidence is increased from 0.45 to 0.55.

node-11.label: Blood and fluid cultures returned negative

node-12.label: Abdominal CT and venous duplex have been requested but results are not yet reported

node-13.label: Acute cardiopulmonary event due to pulmonary embolism with right heart strain

why.why: Both expert analyses specifically favor acute cardiopulmonary event due to pulmonary embolism with right heart strain as the leading hypothesis. Confirmed PE, shock/respiratory failure, and negative cultures all support this mechanism, while pending CTPA and echocardiography prevent definitive confirmation; confidence is increased from 0.55 to 0.65.

node-14.label: Acute cardiopulmonary event due to acute myocardial injury/infarction

attrs.why: The broad frontier can be refined to myocardial injury, which is clinically plausible given shock requiring vasopressors, new atrial fibrillation, and a history of cisplatin/radiation therapy. Cardiac biomarkers and ECG are still pending, so this common cardiopulmonary cause remains a distinct possibility.

node-15.label: Acute cardiopulmonary event due to hemodynamically significant arrhythmia (new atrial fibrillation)

attrs.why: New atrial fibrillation (node-4) with shock and respiratory failure can itself precipitate an acute cardiopulmonary event, either as a primary arrhythmic decompensation or secondary to PE/myocardial injury. ECG is pending, making this a reasonable sub-hypothesis of the broad acute cardiopulmonary event.

node-16.label: Acute cardiopulmonary event due to combined pulmonary embolism and myocardial injury

attrs.why: PE and myocardial injury can coexist in the same acute cardiopulmonary event, especially when right heart strain leads to secondary myocardial ischemia. This combined mechanism is less likely than either alone, but remains plausible until echocardiography, CTPA, and cardiac biomarkers are available.

node-11.label: Blood and fluid cultures returned negative

node-12.label: Abdominal CT and venous duplex have been requested but results are not yet reported

node-13.label: Acute cardiopulmonary event due to pulmonary embolism with right heart strain

why.why: Both expert analyses specifically favor acute cardiopulmonary event due to pulmonary embolism with right heart strain as the leading hypothesis. Confirmed PE, shock/respiratory failure, and negative cultures all support this mechanism, while pending CTPA and echocardiography prevent definitive confirmation; confidence is increased from 0.55 to 0.65.

node-14.label: Acute cardiopulmonary event due to acute myocardial injury/infarction

attrs.why: The broad frontier can be refined to myocardial injury, which is clinically plausible given shock requiring vasopressors, new atrial fibrillation, and a history of cisplatin/radiation therapy. Cardiac biomarkers and ECG are still pending, so this common cardiopulmonary cause remains a distinct possibility.

node-15.label: Acute cardiopulmonary event due to hemodynamically significant arrhythmia (new atrial fibrillation)

attrs.why: New atrial fibrillation (node-4) with shock and respiratory failure can itself precipitate an acute cardiopulmonary event, either as a primary arrhythmic decompensation or secondary to PE/myocardial injury. ECG is pending, making this a reasonable sub-hypothesis of the broad acute cardiopulmonary event.

node-16.label: Acute cardiopulmonary event due to combined pulmonary embolism and myocardial injury

attrs.why: PE and myocardial injury can coexist in the same acute cardiopulmonary event, especially when right heart strain leads to secondary myocardial ischemia. This combined mechanism is less likely than either alone, but remains plausible until echocardiography, CTPA, and cardiac biomarkers are available.
